description.text: Cemex, S.A.B. de C.V. is a publicly traded variable stock corporation (sociedad anónima bursátil de capital variable) organized under the laws of Mexico, with its principal executive offices located at Avenida Ricardo Margáin Zozaya #325, Colonia Valle del Campestre, San Pedro Garza García, Nuevo León, 66265, Mexico. Cemex, S.A.B. de C.V.’s main phone number is +52 81 8888-8888. Our website is located at www.cemex.com. The information on our website is not, and is not intended to be, part of this annual report and is not incorporated into this annual report by reference. Cemex, S.A.B. de C.V. started doing business in 1906 and was registered with the Mercantile Section of the Public Registry of Property and Commerce in Monterrey, Nuevo León, Mexico, on June 11, 1920, which as of the date of this annual report is for an indefinite period. Beginning April 2006, Cemex, S.A.B. de C.V.’s full legal and commercial name is Cemex, Sociedad Anónima Bursátil de Capital Variable. Cemex, S.A.B. de C.V. is an operating and a holding company engaged, directly or indirectly, through its operating subsidiaries, primarily in the production, distribution, marketing and sale of cement, ready-mix concrete, aggregates, clinker, other construction materials and Urbanization Solutions throughout the world. Cemex, S.A.B. de C.V.

about.description_short: Cemex is a multinational construction materials company focused on building a better future for communities worldwide. The company produces and markets cement, ready-mix concrete, aggregates, and related construction materials such as admixtures and mortars, enabling construction projects across its markets. Through customer-centric solutions, operational excellence, and continuous innovation, Cemex delivers high-performance materials that meet the industry's evolving needs. With a workforce of around 40,000 people worldwide, Cemex provides reliable, sustainable, and high-quality products and services, partnering with its customers to deliver solutions that create long-term value. For more information, visit cemex.com and connect with us on LinkedIn.

analysis_md:
# CX — Cemex, S.A.B. de C.V.
First scored run, 2026-10-19, engine release 5.5.0. CX was blocked on 2026-10-17 (DATA_GAP:sbc, escalated NEEDS_MAIN_AGENT) and had never been scored, so no earlier analysis exists. In scope: market cap $15.070B at $10.26 (basis: diluted_latest; price × shares ÷ ads_ratio; nasdaq_quote_api).

Engine figures below are copied from key_numbers.md and dcf_numbers.json of this run; score.json and judgment.json carry the same figures. The ROIC, gross-margin and minority-interest history comes from fundamentals.json and statements.json (WORKER_SPEC step 5). No ttm.json exists for this filer (see Owner's earnings). Figures marked **(research)** come from the company's own releases, cited under Sources. They are context only: no computation uses them.

## What it is
Cemex is one of the largest building-materials groups in the world: cement, ready-mix concrete, aggregates and urban solutions, sold mainly in Mexico, the United States, Europe / Middle East / Africa and South-Central America and the Caribbean. It files a 20-F and reports under IFRS. Since its FY2019 20-F the issuer has presented its statements in U.S. dollars. The engine's FX record names MXN as the reporting currency because the earlier filings were in pesos. One NYSE ADS represents ten CPOs, and each CPO represents three ordinary shares, so one ADS is 30 ordinary shares (judgment.json `ads_ratio`, 20-F Note 1). In 2024–25 it sold the Philippines, the Dominican Republic and Guatemala businesses and its remaining Neoris stake, and these are reported as discontinued operations. Its "Project Cutting Edge" cost programme is running, and management raised its 2026 EBITDA guidance in July 2026 (see the guidance check under DCF).

## Owner's earnings
**Conservative definition: OCF − total capex − SBC.** This is the engine's definition and the base actually used.
- **FY2024 (the base year):** owner's earnings total **$543.0M**, after capex of **$1.296B** (PP&E $1.000B + intangible-asset purchases $296.0M, both read from the 20-F cash-flow statement: `PurchaseOfPropertyPlantAndEquipmentClassifiedAsInvestingActivities` + `PurchaseOfIntangibleAssetsClassifiedAsInvestingActivities`) and SBC of **$55.0M**. The SBC comes from the filing override (see OVERRIDE), because the filer stopped tagging SBC under the engine's IFRS tag after FY2021. Operating cash flow is the filed figure in financials_history.csv (`ocf`).
- FY2023 capex: $1.072B ($865.0M + $207.0M). FY2022 capex: $906.0M ($755.0M + $151.0M). statements.json has the same two cash-flow lines for each year, and they sum to the CSV's `capex`.
- **Base OE/share: $0.37 per ADS** (source: median_of_last_3_fy_oe_per_share). The latest FY OE/share is $0.37 and the 3-yr median is $0.37: FY2024 is itself the median year. Owner's earnings were positive in 5/5 of the last five years.
- **Maintenance definition: NI + D&A − min(capex, D&A) − ΔNWC.** The engine records it in financials_history.csv (`oe_maintenance`), but key_numbers.md does not print it, so it is not quoted here. It runs below the conservative figure in FY2024 and above it in FY2022–FY2023. The Spanish tax fine is not the cause: the 2023 accrual lowered net income and sits in the 2023 working-capital release (`delta_nwc`), so it nets out of NI − ΔNWC just as it nets out of operating cash flow, and the 2024 payment lowers both definitions alike (see NI_OCF_DIVERGENCE). The gap is what separates the filed operating cash-flow line from net income + D&A − the balance-sheet working-capital change, and run outputs do not break it down further. The conservative definition rests on the filed cash-flow line, and it is the one the engine uses.
- **Maintenance vs growth capex:** the conservative figure charges all capex, including strategic and growth capex. For 2026 Cemex guides maintenance capex of about US$900M, strategic capex of about US$210M and growth investments of about US$300M **(research, Q2 2026 release)**. On a maintenance-capex view, owner's earnings would be higher. Under the method the full charge stands, because Cemex's growth spend is recurring rather than one-off.
- **Why the median base and not TTM:** STALE_FY. ttm.py exited 3 ("ocf: no annual (FY) fact; sbc: no annual (FY) fact; shares_diluted: no annual (FY) fact; capex: no capex facts…"). - **What the base contains (cannot be fixed within override authority):**
  1. **A one-off cash payment toward the Spanish tax fine, in FY2024 only.** Cemex adjusted its 2024 free cash flow for a US$383M payment toward a roughly US$500M fine announced in Q4 2023 **(research, FY2024 release)**. The fine was accrued in 2023 and paid in 2024, so only FY2024 operating cash flow carries it, and it *depresses* the base (see NI_OCF_DIVERGENCE). FY2024 is the median year, so the base sits on the one year the fine's payment distorts. The only item in the base pulling the other way is the discontinued-operations cash flow in item 2.
  2. **Cash flow from the discontinued businesses, in all three base years.** The engine's OCF tag (`used_tags.ocf`: `CashFlowsFromUsedInOperatingActivities`) is the 20-F's total line. It includes the operating cash flow of the businesses sold in 2024–25, which the 20-F also files separately (`…DiscontinuedOperations`). `capex_provenance` dates both capex legs for FY2022, FY2023 and FY2024 to the 20-F filed 2025-04-28, but the engine keeps the latest-filed fact for every tag, OCF included, so that date shows only that capex and OCF in these rows come from the same FY2024 20-F. It does not show whether the capex lines are restated to continuing operations: that cannot be verified from the run outputs, and the worker should check the 20-F's investing section. Either way every base year carries the sold businesses' cash flow, which *inflates* the base against a continuing-operations view: by their full operating cash flow if the capex lines are continuing-only, or by their operating cash flow net of their capex if not. No run output prints that slice, because the engine records no OCF provenance and does not read the continuing / discontinued split, so its size is not quoted here. The FY2024 20-F (filed 2025-04-28, consolidated statement of cash flows) is cited for the FY2024 discontinued operating cash flow being smaller than the US$383M tax payment. No run output carries either figure, so that comparison cannot be verified from the run outputs, and the net direction drawn from it below depends on it.

  Net, on the cited reading of the FY2024 20-F (item 2; cannot verify from the run outputs), the FY2024 base understates FY2024 continuing owner's earnings, but not by enough to leave D: correcting both items together keeps the name in D, and only a one-sided correction (the tax payment alone) reaches C. During the independent AGENTS.md audit of this re-score, a sensitivity was run with dcf_engine's own projection and IRR functions, holding g_base, moat and probabilities at this run's inputs. Adding back the tax payment alone lifts the weighted IRR into the C band (10–15%). Removing the discontinued slice as well returns it to D. The slice removed there is the discontinued operating cash flow, which assumes the capex lines are continuing-only (item 2); if they also carry the sold businesses, the slice to remove is smaller and the combined correction lands closer to C. That sensitivity is not an engine output, so its figures are not quoted. Both corrections rest on figures this run does not print: the payment comes from the company's FY2024 release, and the discontinued slice from the 20-F's cash-flow statement. WORKER_SPEC step 8, clause (c), builds a `base_override` only from figures printed in this run's dcf_numbers.json, ttm.json or financials_history.csv, so a corrected base is outside the worker's authority. The base stays as filed, and the question is escalated (see Open items for Andrew).

The 2026-10-19 change is the explicit `currency: "USD"`. The note states the amounts in dollars, and make_score refuses a USD-assumed override at a non-USD reporting filer unless it is declared.

The `_system/overrides_registry.json` entry dated 2026-10-19 records the same impact. score.json sets `exit_alert_eligible: false` ("tier exists only because of a judgment override") and `alert_eligible: false`, so the name is not alert-eligible.

## Moat: 5/10 — moderate / narrow
Justification (judgment.json): local cement and aggregates density, scarce quarries and plants, and high transport costs give Cemex pricing power in its core local markets. But the product is a commodity, ROIC has stayed below 10% through the cycle (judgment.json words it as about 4–10%, but the series below falls to 3.5% in FY2022 and −2.1% in FY2020), and earnings ride construction cycles, energy and carbon costs, and FX.
- **Evidence: ROIC proxy (fundamentals.json `roic_proxy`)**, FY2019 → FY2024: 3.9%, −2.1%, 8.2%, 3.5%, 7.8%, 9.9%. **Gross margin**, same years: 32.8%, 32.2%, 32.2%, 30.5%, 33.7%, 33.6%. Returns have not stayed well above the cost of capital through a cycle. They reached the high single digits only in FY2021 (8.2%) and FY2023–FY2024 (7.8%, 9.9%), with FY2022 back at 3.5% between them. A score of 7 or above would need a reason this history cannot support.
- **FOR:**
  - local-market density: cement is transport-cost bound, roughly a 200–300 km radius, so plant and quarry positions create local oligopolies;
  - scarce permitted quarry reserves and capital-intensive plants deter entry;
  - proven local pricing power, with Mexico cement prices up in local currency in the Q2 2026 prints while volumes grew;
  - scale across Mexico, the US and EMEA, plus a ready-mix and aggregates network that pulls through cement volumes.
- **AGAINST:**
  - ROIC of only 3.5–9.9% over 2022–2024 and negative in 2020;
  - a commodity product whose economics depend on utilisation (high operating leverage);
  - gross margin flat-to-down over the decade, with no expanding pricing-power trend;
  - energy, carbon (EU ETS / CBAM) and decarbonisation capex as structural cost threats;
  - MXN and multi-currency exposure under a USD-priced ADS, plus recurring tax and legal overhangs (the Spanish tax fine).
- A 5 gives **CAP 8.5 years**: growth holds 2 years, then fades to the 2.50% terminal rate.

## DCF (2026-10-19)
Inputs are moat 5, default probabilities 10/25/30/25/10, default offsets and multipliers, and the median base. The growth blend is **4.90% → g_base 4.90%**. Its components are revenue CAGR 5y 4.56%, revenue CAGR 3y 4.05%, latest revenue YoY −2.14% and OE/share CAGR 2y 15.86%. The share-count CAGR is −0.59%, which adds 0.59% to the revenue components only. The 5-year revenue window starts in FY2019 as last filed: the engine keeps each period's latest-filed fact, and `capex_provenance` dates the FY2019 row to the FY2021 20-F filed 2022-04-29. That filing predates the 2024–25 divestitures, so FY2019 still includes the businesses later moved to discontinued operations, and the CAGR slightly understates growth on today's footprint. The OE/share CAGR runs from a low FY2022. The blend sits between the two.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Super bear | 10% | -7.1% | 0.75 | Mexico and US construction downturn plus energy and carbon squeeze; utilisation falls | $1.52 | $1.95 | 4.13% |
| Bear | 25% | -0.1% | 0.9 | 2026 recovery fades; flat volumes; carbon costs absorb the savings | $2.45 | $3.20 | 5.40% |
| Base | 30% | 4.9% | 1.0 | Mid-single-digit growth on pricing and cost savings, fading over the CAP | $3.35 | $4.43 | 6.66% |
| Bull | 25% | 9.9% | 1.1 | Cutting Edge savings stick, Mexico recovers, US infrastructure demand holds | $4.53 | $6.07 | 8.28% |
| Super bull | 10% | 16.9% | 1.25 | 2026's guided EBITDA jump carries through to owner's earnings for several years | $6.85 | $9.34 | 11.23% |

- **Probability-weighted:** IV@15% **$3.59** (upside −65.0%), IV@12% $4.78 (−53.4%), IV@10% $6.11. Weighted IRR **7.03%**; base-case IRR 6.66%.
- **Band:** bear 5.40% (tier D) → bull 8.28% (tier D); scenario range 4.13% – 11.23%. **Tier by numbers: D.**
- **Diagnostics:** OE yield 3.60%; terminal value 19.0% of IV@15; scenario spread 4.51x; net debt / normalized OE 8.59x; 21.6 months since FY end.
- **Guidance-vs-model check (WORKER_SPEC step 4):** in July 2026 Cemex raised its full-year 2026 EBITDA guidance to growth of 16% to 17%, from high single digits **(research, Q2 2026 release)**. The base-case start (4.9%) and the bull start (9.9%) sit below that one-year EBITDA guide. Only the super bull (16.9%) is in line with it. These starts are kept for four reasons:
  - The guide is one year of *EBITDA* recovering from a flat FY2025 (EBITDA growth about 1% for the year **(research, FY2025 release)**). The scenario start is a sustained *owner's-earnings-per-share* rate that holds for 2 years and then fades to the terminal rate over the 8.5-year CAP.
  - Part of the EBITDA gain is one-off cost savings, which raise the level once and do not compound.
  - The 2026 plan raises capex and growth investment, which the conservative definition charges.
  - Cemex's EBITDA has swung with the cycle, as the ROIC history above shows.

  The guide makes the *base level* stale. It does not make the growth rate wrong. That is handled under STALE_FY and in the verdict, not by raising the starts.

## Flags — every fragility flag resolved
- **STALE_FY** (21.6 months since the FY2024 year end). Cemex has filed its FY2025 20-F: its cover-page count, dated 2025-12-31, is in dcf_numbers.json `share_basis`, and segments.py read the FY2025 XBRL instance. But EDGAR companyfacts carries none of that 20-F's financial statements. fundamentals.py and statements.py both warn that the latest 20-F "is not yet in EDGAR companyfacts" and stop at 2024-12-31. ttm.py exited 3 (IFRS filer, no 10-Qs). The quarterly 6-K releases print free cash flow and capex, but a base built from them would use figures this run does not print, which is outside WORKER_SPEC step 8, clause (c). **Resolution:** the FY2024-centred median base is used and named as stale, and whether a filing-sourced base is allowed here is escalated (see Open items for Andrew). The FY2025 release reports free cash flow from operations of about US$1.2B, up about 50% on an adjusted basis **(research)**. Together with the 2026 guide, this points to current owner's earnings *above* the base, so the stale base biases the IRR down, not up (see verdict). Re-score when companyfacts carries the FY2025 20-F.
- **NI_OCF_DIVERGENCE** (2023). **Resolution: 2023 net income is held down by an out-of-line tax charge, of which the Spanish tax fine is only part, and FY2023 does not set the base.** The 2023 gap is $2,023M (CSV: `ocf` $2,222M against `net_income` $199M). D&A of $1,190M and a working-capital release of $916M (`delta_nwc` −$916M), less $83M of other items, reconcile the two. The 2023 `tax` line is $1,204M, against $168M in 2022 and $67M in 2024, so 2023 carries about $1.0B more tax expense than either neighbouring year. Part of that is the roughly US$500M fine announced in Q4 2023 **(research, FY2024 release)**, which went through 2023 income-tax expense but was not paid in 2023: a charge accrued but not paid lowers net income and raises a liability by the same amount, so it is part of the 2023 working-capital release and leaves operating cash flow unchanged. The fine is only about half of the excess tax charge, and the run outputs do not break down the rest (whether it too was unpaid or non-cash cannot be verified from the run outputs; the worker should check the FY2023 20-F income-tax note). Removing a US$500M accrual still leaves a gap of about $1,523M, more than 40% of OCF and more than D&A, so the flag would still fire under the engine's rule: the fine is one cause of the divergence, not all of it. For the base, FY2023 is the highest of the three years (OE $1.095B against $543.0M in FY2024 and $407.0M in FY2022), so it is not the median year and does not set the base. If part of the $916M release were a one-off cash inflow rather than an unpaid charge, FY2023 owner's earnings would be overstated; that would move the base only if the correction exceeded about $550M (FY2023 less FY2024, on near-equal share counts), and then it would lower it. The fine's cash left in 2024, when Cemex paid US$383M of it **(research, FY2024 release)**, and that payment depresses FY2024 OCF. FY2024 is the median year, so the base sits on the one year the payment distorts; the discontinued-operations cash flow in the same row works the other way (see Owner's earnings, item 2). The net direction carried into the verdict (base understated) rests on the cited reading of the FY2024 20-F described there, which cannot be verified from the run outputs.
- **FX_CONVERTED** (reporting currency MXN; ECB period-end rates). **Resolution: immaterial to the valuation.** `fx_conversion.rates` records rates only for period ends 2014-12-31 to 2017-12-31. The 2015–2017 rates line up with the three oldest history rows (financials_history.csv starts at 2015-12-31); 2014-12-31 is not a history row. The base window (FY2022–FY2024) and the growth windows use the issuer's own USD figures.
- **USD_TRANSLATIONS_USED.** **Resolution:** since its FY2019 20-F, Cemex presents its statements in U.S. dollars, and the engine used those filed USD figures. This is the basis on which the SBC override is declared `currency: "USD"` and used verbatim.
- **ADS_RATIO_APPLIED** (x30.0). **Resolution:** the ratio is stated in the filer's own 20-F (Note 1: 3 ordinary shares per CPO, 10 CPOs per ADS) and is corroborated by Note 21. Per-share figures are per ADS, and the cap divides by the ratio: $15.070B on 44,065,652,000 diluted ordinary shares. The cover-page count, 14,507,429,244 (dei_to_shares 0.329223), counts CPOs, not ordinary shares. That is consistent with three shares per CPO, so the engine recorded it and did not apply it.
- **OVERRIDE_APPLIED:sbc.** See OVERRIDE: a filing source with currency declared, $55.0M, an impact of −9.20% on the base and −0.45pp on the IRR, and it unblocks the tier.
- **WIDE_SCENARIO_SPREAD** (4.51x). **Resolution:** this is real cyclicality, a commodity business at high operating leverage. Confidence is **low**, not high. Every scenario, including the super bull at 11.23%, is below the 15% hurdle, so the spread does not change the conclusion.
- **HIGH_NET_DEBT** (net debt / normalized OE 8.59x). **Resolution:** net debt is $4.665B: long-term plus current borrowings less cash (`net_debt_basis`), which ties to the FY2024 20-F balance-sheet tags. Lease liabilities are outside it (`lease_liabilities_latest` null), and so are the subordinated perpetual notes the 20-F carries apart from borrowings. Leverage is therefore *higher* than the ratio shows. The denominator, the FY2024 base, is depressed by the tax payment and lifted by the discontinued slice; on the cited reading of the FY2024 20-F the net effect depresses it (cannot verify from the run outputs; see Owner's earnings), which would inflate the ratio, but the leverage is a real constraint: the bear cases (5.40%, super bear 4.13%) are where a levered cement company lands in a downturn. That is one more reason to size to the bear end, which is D anyway.
- **Minority interests** (method limit, not a flag): owner's earnings are consolidated. Non-controlling interests, mainly the listed Caribbean subsidiaries (the Trinidad Cement group), are a small part of equity and profit in the 20-F: statements.json shows non-controlling interests of $301M against total equity of $12.477B at 2024-12-31. The base is not reduced for them, which is a small upward bias.

## My thoughts / overlay
- The method's answer is clear on hurdles and narrow on tier. No defensible base gets Cemex to 15% at $10.26. The hurdle-clearing prices are 15% at $3.59, 20% at $2.52 and 25% at $1.93. The D/C line is the honest uncertainty. The mechanical median lands on the year the Spanish tax fine was paid, and the 2025–26 recovery is not in the filed data yet.
- Quality: a moderate local-oligopoly moat, now with capex fully counted (intangible purchases included) and SBC charged at the filed figures. Owner's earnings have been positive 5/5 years, but they are thin against $4.665B of net debt (8.59x) before leases and hybrids.
- Watch items: the FY2025 20-F reaching companyfacts (re-score trigger); the Q3 2026 release, which is not yet out as of this run; the remaining Spanish tax-fine balance; the US$500M buyback over three years and the higher dividend **(research, FY2025 release)**, which compete with deleveraging; and carbon costs in EMEA.
- Margin of safety: none. The weighted IV@15% sits 65.0% below the price, and even IV@10% ($6.11) is below it.

## Final verdict
- **Final tier: D** (numbers tier; weighted IRR 7.03%; band D → D). No tier override.
- **Confidence: low.** Four reasons:
  - the base year is 21.6 months stale and contains a one-off tax payment and discontinued-operations cash flow;
  - SBC in all three base years comes from a filing override;
  - WIDE_SCENARIO_SPREAD;
  - HIGH_NET_DEBT, with leases and hybrids outside net debt.
- **One-liner (score.json):** Tier D: moat 5/10 local-density cement incumbent with ROIC of roughly 4-10% - on the last filed year (FY2024, 22 months stale, base $0.37/ADS once engine 5.5 adds intangible-asset purchases to capex) the weighted IRR is 7.03% at $10.26 with the whole band in D; clears 15% only at $3.59 (IV@15). A FY2025 base may lift it toward C, not near B. (Its "roughly 4-10%" is loose: the fundamentals.json series under Moat runs from −2.1% to 9.9%.)
